source.title: Learning and Forgetting Unsafe Examples in Large Language Models
source.authors: Jia-Chen Zhao; Zhun Deng; David Madras; James Zou; Mengye Ren

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically examines whether fine-tuning on noisy data containing unsafe examples changes safety-related behavior, using bias and toxicity measures rather than refusal rates or harmful-request compliance.
record.gate_note: The study does not measure refusal on harmful user requests, benign-only fine-tuning effects, per-token KL, opening-token bypasses, safety-localized parameters, or safety-depth training. Its bias and toxicity outcomes are related safety measures, not the behaviors named by the claim versions, so the rows below use versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study does not test any claim version. Its own results are bias (BBQ) and toxicity (Detoxify) scores after fine-tuning on noisy data with 50% unsafe examples. Those are related but different constructs from compliance with harmful user requests (V1/V2). HarmfulQA appears only in forgetting-rate experiments, with no compliance measure. The 'aligned' models are LLaMA-7B and GPT-2 models the authors trained themselves on safe examples, not standard safety-trained chat models. The original fine-tuning-attack finding (Qi et al.) is mentioned only as concurrent work. The record's relation 'tests'/T2 contradicts its own gate note, in which every version is not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Missing the central finding: during safety fine-tuning, unsafe examples are forgotten more than other data. This disparity grows with model size, is absent in GPT2-M, and vanishes when the safe data is of a different safety category. ForgetFilter exploits this disparity to filter unsafe data.
record.recipe_differences: Studies noisy downstream fine-tuning and subsequent safety fine-tuning using bias, toxicity, and forgetting measures; it does not use the few-example refusal, token-KL, or opening-prefill methods in the cited original sources.
record.method_sensitivity: The forgetting disparity depends on model size and on whether safe review examples match the unsafe-data safety category; the authors report no observable disparity under the tested toxic-to-unbiased domain shift. Toxicity learning is described as similar across model scales, while bias learning is faster in larger models.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning self-aligned LLaMA-7B on noisy data with 50% biased or toxic examples raises bias from 0.00 to 0.57 and toxicity from 0.03 to 0.45 (Table 2). Figure 2 shows similar rises for GPT-2 M/L/XL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fine-tuning on downstream data containing unsafe examples raises bias/toxicity in previously safety-tuned models.

fits_no_version.finding: After safety fine-tuning, bias returns immediately when noisy data is presented again and grows over interleaved sessions (Figure 5). Self-correction prompting also degrades over time.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety re-fine-tuning suppresses but does not erase learned unsafe behaviour, which is rapidly recalled on re-exposure.

fits_no_version.finding: Sequential safety fine-tuning restores low bias/toxicity (0.01/0.05) but costs downstream F1 (82.4 to 75.7 on bias). Replay barely helps (toxicity 0.43).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc safety fine-tuning recovers safety at a cost to downstream capability.

record.problems: The relevant behavioral outcomes are bias and toxicity scores rather than harmful-request refusal or compliance. Figure 2 and Figure 5 provide curves without exact textual values; no uncertainty estimates are stated in the reported results.
record.rows_left_out: Forgetting-rate comparisons and ForgetFilter classification F1 results were omitted because they measure retention or filtering performance, not the claim versions’ named response behavior. Downstream-task F1 results were also omitted. Sections 2.2.1, 2.3, Table 1, Figure 3, and Figure 4 report these results.

untested.parts: No harmful-request compliance or refusal measure after harmful fine-tuning. Unsafe data is 2,500 biased/toxic examples, far more than a few hundred, given to self-aligned models.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
No localization of safety parameters. Appendix B finetunes only the top block, but for forgetting rates, not safety localization.
No test of why alignment is shallow.
No deepening method. The interleaved-training recall of bias concerns re-fine-tuning, not token depth.

record.verdict_notes: The record's relation and tranche ('tests', T2) are inconsistent with its own gate note, in which all versions are not tested; corrected to discusses/T6. The bias/toxicity outcomes are a related construct, not harmful-request compliance. The models are aligned by the authors' own safe-example fine-tuning, not standard RLHF/safety-trained chat models. Harmfulness has no output metric in the paper.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure compliance with harmful requests or refusal after harmful-example fine-tuning.
Does not test ordinary or carefully selected benign-only fine-tuning for increased harmful-request compliance.
Does not compare aligned and base models’ per-token KL across response positions.
Does not test compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes as bypasses.
Does not test whether safety is localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
Does not test whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response tokens.
